0.title: Christ Is All: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
0.overview:
Colossians is the most christologically concentrated letter in the Pauline corpus. Its central argument can be stated in five words: Christ is all you need. The church at Colossae was being seduced by a sophisticated religious system — a blend of Jewish legal observance, angel veneration, ascetic practices, and esoteric philosophy that scholars call the “Colossian heresy.” The false teachers were not asking the Colossians to abandon Christ; they were proposing to supplement him, to add the fullness they implied Christ alone could not provide. Paul’s response is the great Christ hymn of chapter 1 and the devastating theological logic of chapter 2: in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (2:9–10). There is nothing to add. He is enough.

Paul wrote the letter from prison, most likely in Rome, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon — the so-called “Prison Epistles.” The church at Colossae had apparently been founded not by Paul himself but by Epaphras (1:7), one of Paul’s co-workers, during Paul’s extended ministry in Ephesus (Acts 19). Paul had never visited the church personally (2:1), and yet he writes with the pastoral urgency of a father: he is “struggling” for them (2:1), praying that they would have “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” hidden in Christ (2:3), warning them against the plausible-sounding deception that threatens to take them captive (2:8).

The letter’s structure is elegant. Chapters 1–2 are theological: the supremacy of Christ over all creation (1:15–20), the mystery of Christ in you as the hope of glory (1:27), and the fullness of deity in Christ as the demolition of every religious supplement (2:9–15). Chapters 3–4 are ethical: if Christ is everything, if you have died and been raised with him, if your life is hidden with him in God, then certain things must be put to death and certain things must be put on. The theology of chapters 1–2 always produces the ethics of chapters 3–4 in Pauline thought. Indicative before imperative; who you are before what you do.

The Christ hymn of Colossians 1:15–20 is one of the most majestic texts in the entire New Testament. In six verses it covers the entire scope of Christ’s lordship: he is the image of the invisible God; the firstborn over all creation; the one through whom, for whom, and in whom all things were created and cohere; the head of the body; the firstborn from the dead; the one in whom all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell; the one through whom God reconciled all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross. This is not merely elevated religious poetry; it is the most comprehensive christological statement in Paul’s letters, and it provides the theological foundation for everything else the letter argues. If Christ is who the hymn says he is, then the Colossian heresy — and every supplement to Christ in every generation — is not merely unnecessary but absurd.

Did Paul write Colossians? Some scholars doubt it, pointing to vocabulary and style unlike his undisputed letters, to the soaring hymn of 1:15–20, and to its close relation to Ephesians. But the letter names Paul three times (1:1, 23; 4:18), closes with his own signature, and is tied by its list of names to Philemon, which almost no one doubts is his. Differences of style are well explained by the subject, a new error to answer, and by the help of a co-writer, Timothy (1:1). The church received it as Paul’s from the beginning, and the more likely conclusion is that he wrote it.

Colossians is the answer to every form of Christianity that adds to Christ. It speaks directly to the believer who feels that faith in Christ alone is not quite enough — that additional spiritual experiences, additional practices, additional revelations are needed for full access to God. The letter says: you have been filled in him. You are complete. The fullness you are seeking is already yours, in the one in whom all fullness dwells. Seek more of him — not more beyond him.

1.title: The Supremacy of Christ: Hymn, Mystery, and Ministry
1.overview:
Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus. Paul had never visited; the church was planted by Epaphras, a local man converted probably during Paul’s years in Ephesus. Now, writing from prison, Paul hears that teachers are offering the Colossians something “more”: secret knowledge, angelic powers to be honoured, food laws and festivals, and harsh treatment of the body (2:8–23). Paul’s answer is not a better technique but a bigger Christ.

Chapter 1 thanks God for their faith, love and hope, and prays that they will know God’s will so as to live worthily, strengthened by his power, thankful that the Father has already qualified, rescued, transferred, redeemed and forgiven them. Then comes the great hymn (vv. 15–20): Christ is the image of the invisible God, the Creator and sustainer of everything, including every spiritual power; the head of the church and firstborn from the dead; the one in whom all God’s fullness dwells, who made peace by the blood of his cross. Finally Paul applies it: you who were God’s enemies are reconciled, if you continue in the faith, and the great mystery now revealed is “Christ in you, the hope of glory”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul had not founded himself; it was planted by Epaphras. Paul thanks God for their faith in Christ and their love for all believers, both springing from the hope stored up for them in heaven, which they heard in the gospel now bearing fruit across the world. He prays that God will fill them with knowledge of his will, so that they live in a way that honours the Lord, growing in good works and in knowing God, strengthened to endure with patience and joy, and thankful to the Father, who has rescued them from the power of darkness and brought them into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom they have redemption and forgiveness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Knowledge of God’s Will: Wisdom vs. Esoteric Speculation

Paul’s prayer for “knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (v. 9) directly counters the false teachers’ offer of special knowledge. The knowledge Paul seeks for the Colossians is not mystical or esoteric; it is practical and ethical: “so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord.” Reformed theology has always insisted that true wisdom is not the accumulation of specialized spiritual information but the God-given capacity to live well in the world as God has made it, according to God’s own revealed will. The wisdom from above, as James says (3:17), is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits.” It is visible in life, not in the possession of secret knowledge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered a form of spiritual wisdom that was speculative, esoteric, and attainable only through special initiation. Paul’s prayer shows what genuine spiritual wisdom looks like: it produces fruit, builds endurance, and generates thanksgiving. Now: The contemporary church is perennially attracted to special spiritual knowledge — prophetic insights, mystical experiences, hidden wisdom that the ordinary believer does not possess. Paul’s prayer is the corrective: true knowledge of God’s will is measured not by the height of its claims but by the quality of life it produces. Does it make you fruitful? Does it make you endure? Does it make you thankful? Those are the tests.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.

Meaning first. Colossians is Paul’s great letter on the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ. A teaching had appeared at Colossae that added to Christ: special knowledge, mystical visions, the worship of angels, food laws and festivals. Paul’s answer is to show how great Christ is, so that believers need nothing more. Chapter 1 has four movements. First, thanksgiving for the Colossians’ faith, love and hope, and for the gospel bearing fruit among them (vv. 1–8). Second, a prayer that they will be filled with knowledge of God’s will, live worthily, be strengthened with endurance and give thanks to the Father, who has rescued them from darkness into the kingdom of his Son (vv. 9–14). Third, one of the Bible’s highest passages on Christ: he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over creation, the one through whom and for whom all things were made and hold together, the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead, in whom all God’s fullness dwells, and through whom God reconciled all things by the blood of his cross (vv. 15–20). Fourth, the application: the Colossians, once enemies, are now reconciled, if they continue in the faith; and Paul gladly suffers to make known the mystery, Christ in you, the hope of glory, so that he may present everyone mature in Christ (vv. 21–29).

Setting and background. Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13). Once important, it had declined. Paul had never visited (2:1). The church was founded by Epaphras, probably during Paul’s three years in Ephesus (Acts 19:10). Paul writes from prison, probably Rome around AD 60–62, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon, sending the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus (4:7–9).

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. Key words. Paul writes to a church that does not know him personally, so he states his authority: from God’s will, not his own.

And Timothy our brother. Key words. Timothy was with Paul in prison.

To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae. Key words. Saints: set apart for God. Faithful: believing and trustworthy. In Christ: their true location. At Colossae: their earthly address. Every believer has both.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father. Key words. Paul’s greeting. Here only the Father is named; Christ fills the rest of the letter.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only special Christians are saints. All believers are.

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to God’s holy people in Colossae, the faithful brothers and sisters in Christ: grace and peace to you from God our Father.

On a Tuesday. You live at two addresses: in Christ, and in your town. Let the first shape how you live at the second.
verseByVerse.note: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited; the church was founded by Epaphras. Paul wrote from prison, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon.

verseByVerse.quote: We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,

We always thank God. Key words. Paul begins with thanks for a church he has never seen. Thanksgiving is a theme of the letter (1:12; 2:7; 3:15–17; 4:2).

The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. God is known as Father through his Son. Christ’s relationship to the Father is eternal and unique.

When we pray for you. Key words. Paul’s thanks rise in his prayers. He prayed regularly for churches far away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul thanked God for everything about them. He goes on to warn them. But he starts with God’s work.

In a sentence. We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,

For worship. Thank God today for the faith of believers in another church or country.

verseByVerse.quote: since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints,

Since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus. Key words. Epaphras had reported it (v. 8). Faith in Christ: resting in him, the object of faith.

And of the love that you have for all the saints. Key words. Faith in Christ shows itself in love for his people, all of them, not just some (Galatians 5:6; 1 John 4:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean love earns salvation. It is the fruit of faith.

In a sentence. because we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love you have for all God’s people,

On a Tuesday. Is your faith visible in love for all believers, including the difficult ones?

verseByVerse.quote: because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,

Because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Key words. The source of faith and love: hope. Not wishful thinking, but the certain future God has prepared. “Laid up” (apokeimai, stored, reserved, kept safe, 2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 1:4). The famous triad of faith, love and hope (1 Corinthians 13:13). Hope fuels faith and love: those sure of heaven can afford to love sacrificially on earth.

Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel. Key words. They heard of this hope when the gospel first came to them. The gospel is the word of the truth: not one opinion among many, but the truth. The false teachers offered something “more”; Paul reminds them that what they first heard was the truth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian hope is only for the future. It shapes life now.

In a sentence. the faith and love that spring from the hope stored up for you in heaven and about which you have already heard in the true message of the gospel

For worship. Your hope is stored safely in heaven. Thank God that no one can steal it.

verseByVerse.quote: which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,

Which has come to you. Key words. The gospel travelled to them, as it travels everywhere.

As indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing. Key words. Like a living plant, the gospel grows and spreads (Mark 4:8; Acts 6:7; 12:24). Bearing fruit: changing lives. Increasing: spreading to new people. The whole world: not a local cult or secret teaching, but a worldwide message. This contrasts with the false teaching, which was for an elite few.

As it also does among you, since the day you heard it. Key words. The same gospel, at work among them from the first day.

And understood the grace of God in truth. Key words. “Understood” (epiginōskō, came to know fully). They grasped that salvation is God’s grace, not human achievement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in the world had heard. It means the gospel was spreading everywhere.

In a sentence. that has come to you. In the same way, the gospel is bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, just as it has been doing among you since the day you heard it and truly understood God’s grace.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is still bearing fruit worldwide. Pray for its growth in a nation you care about.

verseByVerse.quote: just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf
verseByVerse.commentary:
just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf

Just as you learned it from Epaphras. Key words. Epaphras was a native of Colossae who probably heard the gospel from Paul in Ephesus, then took it home (4:12–13). Paul endorses his teaching: what you learned from him is the true gospel. Do not abandon it for the new teachers.

Our beloved fellow servant. Key words. “Fellow servant” (syndoulos, fellow slave). Paul honours him as an equal in service.

He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf. Key words. “Minister” (diakonos). Some manuscripts read “on our behalf,” as the ESV notes: Epaphras represented Paul among them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gospel depends on the messenger. It means faithful messengers deserve honour.

In a sentence. You learned it from Epaphras, our dear fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf,

For worship. Thank God for the person who first brought you the gospel. Pray for them, or thank them.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphras was a native of Colossae who probably heard the gospel during Paul’s long stay in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.

And has made known to us your love in the Spirit. Key words. Epaphras reported their love. In the Spirit: love produced by the Holy Spirit (Galatians 5:22; Romans 5:5). The only mention of the Spirit in Colossians, which focuses on Christ. The Spirit’s work is to make Christ known and produce love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit is unimportant in Colossians. His work is assumed throughout.

In a sentence. and who also told us of your love in the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Ask the Spirit to produce love in you today, for someone specific.

verseByVerse.quote: And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,

And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you. Key words. Constant prayer for people he had never met.

Asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will. Key words. The false teachers promised special knowledge (gnōsis). Paul prays for true knowledge (epignōsis, full knowledge) of God’s will: what he has revealed about salvation and how to live.

In all spiritual wisdom and understanding. Key words. Wisdom (sophia): seeing life from God’s viewpoint. Understanding (synesis): putting things together, applying truth. Spiritual: given by the Spirit. Not secret knowledge for a few, but wisdom for all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean seeking private revelations about God’s will for every decision. God’s will is revealed in Scripture, and wisdom applies it.

In a sentence. For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you. We continually ask God to fill you with the knowledge of his will through all the wisdom and understanding that the Spirit gives,

For worship. Pray this prayer for yourself: Lord, fill me with the knowledge of your will.

verseByVerse.quote: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;

So as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord. Key words. The purpose of knowledge is conduct. “Walk”: daily life. Worthy: fitting for those who belong to such a Lord.

Fully pleasing to him. Key words. “Fully pleasing” (areskeia, desire to please). The aim of life: to please Christ (2 Corinthians 5:9).

Bearing fruit in every good work. Key words. Like the gospel (v. 6), believers bear fruit: good works flowing from new life (Ephesians 2:10).

And increasing in the knowledge of God. Key words. Knowledge leads to obedience, and obedience to more knowledge (John 7:17). A cycle of growth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s approval by our works. We are already accepted in Christ. We now aim to please him as children please a father.

In a sentence. so that you may live a life worthy of the Lord and please him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God,

On a Tuesday. Ask before each task today: how can I please the Lord in this?

verseByVerse.quote: being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;
verseByVerse.commentary:
being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;

Being strengthened with all power. Key words. “Strengthened” (dynamoō). God’s power at work in believers.

According to his glorious might. Key words. Not according to our weakness, but his might, the power of his glory.

For all endurance and patience with joy. Key words. Surprising: God’s mighty power is given not for spectacular feats, but for endurance (hypomonē, bearing up under trials) and patience (makrothymia, bearing with people). With joy: not grim endurance. Patience with joy is a miracle of grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God removes trials. It means he gives strength to endure them joyfully.

In a sentence. being strengthened with all power according to his glorious might so that you may have great endurance and patience, and joyfully

For worship. Ask God for his glorious power, not to escape your trial, but to endure it with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.

Giving thanks to the Father. Key words. Thankfulness, the fruit of grace.

Who has qualified you. Key words. “Qualified” (hikanoō, made sufficient, made fit). The false teachers said believers needed more to qualify: special rituals and knowledge. Paul says: the Father has already qualified you. Nothing more is needed.

To share in the inheritance of the saints in light. Key words. Like Israel’s inheritance of the promised land, believers share an inheritance: eternal life in God’s kingdom. In light: the realm of God’s holiness and truth (1 John 1:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we qualified ourselves. The Father did it, through Christ.

In a sentence. giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of his holy people in the kingdom of light.

On a Tuesday. When you feel unqualified before God, remember: the Father has qualified you in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,

He has delivered us from the domain of darkness. Key words. “Delivered” (rhyomai, rescued). “Domain” (exousia, authority, power). Before Christ, we were under Satan’s authority (Ephesians 2:2; Acts 26:18). God rescued us.

And transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son. Key words. “Transferred” (methistēmi), a word used of deporting whole populations from one country to another. God moved us from one kingdom to another. The kingdom of his beloved Son: Christ reigns now over his people. Past tense: already done.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are free from all spiritual struggle. But Satan has no rightful authority over them.

In a sentence. For he has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son he loves,

For worship. Thank God that you have been moved from darkness into the kingdom of his beloved Son. You belong there now.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

In whom we have redemption. Key words. “Redemption” (apolytrōsis, release by payment of a ransom). In Christ, we are freed. Some later manuscripts add “through his blood,” from Ephesians 1:7.

The forgiveness of sins. Key words. Redemption defined: forgiveness. Our debts cancelled (2:13–14). Not something to be achieved by rituals or experiences, as the false teachers implied, but something believers already have in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean redemption is only future. We have it now.

In a sentence. in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

On a Tuesday. You are forgiven. Live free of guilt today.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In what may be an early Christian hymn, Paul describes who Christ is. He makes the invisible God visible. He holds the rank of the firstborn over all creation, because everything, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, including every spiritual power, was made through him and for him. He existed before all things and holds them together. He is also head of the church, the first to rise from the dead, so that he has first place in everything. The whole fullness of God was pleased to live in him, and through him God made peace with all things by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as Creator and Redeemer: The Cosmic Scope of the Gospel

The Reformed tradition has always insisted on the unity of Christ’s work as both the agent of creation and the author of redemption. The hymn of Colossians 1:15–20 grounds this insistence: the same one through whom all things were made is the one through whose blood all things are reconciled. This means that redemption is not the rescue of souls from a material world that God has abandoned; it is the renewal of the entire creation that God originally made through Christ. The scope of the atonement is cosmic, not merely individual; the goal of redemption is “all things,” not merely individual souls. Abraham Kuyper’s famous claim — “there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: ‘Mine!’” — is exegetically grounded here.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian heresy apparently involved a hierarchy of spiritual powers — angels, thrones, dominions, rulers — through whom one had to navigate to reach God. The hymn annihilates this hierarchy: all these powers were created by Christ, are sustained by Christ, and are subject to Christ. There is no mediating hierarchy between the believer and God; Christ is the direct and only mediator. Now: Every form of Christianity that introduces additional mediators — saints, angels, spiritual powers, ecclesiastical hierarchies — between the believer and God is doing what the Colossian heresy did. The hymn says: Christ is the image of the invisible God. To see God, look at Christ. To reach God, come through Christ. There is no other way, no additional hierarchy, no further mediation required.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.

The Christ hymn. Verses 15–20 are often thought to be an early Christian hymn, in two stanzas: Christ and creation (vv. 15–17), Christ and the new creation (vv. 18–20). It is one of the highest statements of Christ’s person in Scripture, aimed at a teaching that made Christ one spiritual power among many.

He is the image of the invisible God. Key words. “Image” (eikōn): not a mere copy, but the exact representation and revelation. God is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17; John 1:18), but in Christ the invisible God is made visible (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3; 2 Corinthians 4:4). Adam was made in God’s image; Christ is God’s image.

The firstborn of all creation. Key words. “Firstborn” (prōtotokos) speaks of rank and supremacy, as the heir held first place in the family. Not first created, but first in rank, heir and ruler over all creation. God called Israel his firstborn (Exodus 4:22) and David his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth (Psalm 89:27), though David was the youngest son. “Of all creation” means over all creation, as verse 16 explains: because all things were created by him.

Where Christians differ: is Christ a created being? Ancient Arians and modern Jehovah’s Witnesses take firstborn to mean that Christ was the first being God created, through whom he made everything else. Verdict: Verse 16 gives the reason he is firstborn: “for by him all things were created.” If he created all things, he is not one of them. Firstborn here means supreme heir, not first created; Paul had another word for “first created” and did not use it. And verse 19 says all the fullness of God dwells in him. Christ is the eternal Son, uncreated, fully God, of one substance with the Father (John 1:1–3; Nicene Creed).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ had a beginning. He is before all things (v. 17).

In a sentence. The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation.

For worship. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus. Worship him as the image of the invisible God.
verseByVerse.note: “Firstborn” speaks of rank and supremacy, as the heir held first place — not that the Son was created.

parallels.desc: I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities — all things were created through him and for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him.

For by him all things were created. Key words. “By him” (literally in him): creation happened in the sphere of the Son. All things: no exceptions. Christ is the Creator (John 1:3; Hebrews 1:2).

In heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. Key words. The whole universe, seen and unseen.

Whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. Key words. Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers, angels good and evil, which the false teachers honoured or feared (2:15, 18). Christ made them all. They are his creatures, under him.

All things were created through him and for him. Key words. Through him: he is the agent of creation. For him: he is its goal. Everything exists for Christ’s glory. Only God can be the purpose of creation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father did not create. The Father created through the Son, by the Spirit.

In a sentence. For in him all things were created: things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or powers or rulers or authorities; all things have been created through him and for him.

On a Tuesday. You were made for Christ. So was everything you see today. Live accordingly.
verseByVerse.note: Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.

And he is before all things. Key words. Before in time, existing eternally; and before in rank. “Is,” not “was”: eternal present (John 8:58).

And in him all things hold together. Key words. “Hold together” (synistēmi, cohere, are sustained). Christ upholds the universe moment by moment (Hebrews 1:3). Atoms, galaxies, laws of nature: all held together by him. Without him, everything would fall apart.

What it does not mean. It does not mean scientific explanation is unimportant. It means the order science discovers is sustained by Christ.

In a sentence. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together.

For worship. The one who holds the universe together holds your life together. Trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.

And he is the head of the body, the church. Key words. The second stanza: Christ and the new creation. As head, he gives the church life, unity and direction, and rules it (Ephesians 1:22–23; 4:15–16). The church depends on him as a body on its head.

He is the beginning. Key words. “Beginning” (archē, origin, source, ruler). The source of the new creation.

The firstborn from the dead. Key words. The first to rise from the dead to resurrection life, never to die again (1 Corinthians 15:20; Revelation 1:5). First in rank among the raised. His resurrection guarantees ours.

That in everything he might be preeminent. Key words. “Preeminent” (prōteuō, be first). First in creation, first in new creation. First in everything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ needs the church to be complete. The church needs him.

In a sentence. And he is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning and the firstborn from among the dead, so that in everything he might have the supremacy.

On a Tuesday. Is Christ first in everything in your life: your time, money, relationships, ambitions? Give him first place.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,

For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell. Key words. “Fullness” (plērōma): perhaps a word the false teachers used for the totality of divine powers, spread out among angels and spirits. Paul says: all the fullness of God, the entire divine nature, dwells in Christ (2:9). Not partly, not a share. “Dwell” (katoikeō, take up permanent residence). God was pleased to do it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the fullness came to dwell in him at some point, as if he were not God before. It speaks of the incarnate Son, in whom the eternal God fully dwells in bodily form.

In a sentence. For God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him,

For worship. All of God is in Christ. You need nothing beyond him.

verseByVerse.quote: and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.

And through him to reconcile to himself all things. Key words. Sin brought disorder and enmity into creation. Through Christ, God restores harmony. “Reconcile” (apokatallassō, fully reconcile, change from enmity to peace).

Whether on earth or in heaven. Key words. The whole cosmos, which was created through him, is brought back under him.

Making peace by the blood of his cross. Key words. The means: not special knowledge or angel worship, but Christ’s sacrificial death. The cross is the centre of cosmic history.

Where Christians differ: will all things, including all people and demons, be saved? Some read “reconcile all things” as universal salvation. Verdict: Paul means that Christ restores all creation to its proper order under God. Believers are reconciled as friends (vv. 21–22); hostile powers are pacified by being disarmed and defeated (2:15), not saved. The same Paul teaches eternal judgement (2 Thessalonians 1:9). The whole universe will be brought back into peace with God, with evil judged and removed, and creation itself set free (Romans 8:19–21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person will be saved regardless of faith. Reconciliation is received through faith (v. 23).

In a sentence. and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through his blood, shed on the cross.

On a Tuesday. The cross is bringing peace to the whole universe. Be a peacemaker today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — Reconciled and the Mystery Revealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Colossians were once estranged from God and hostile, as their actions showed. Now God has reconciled them through Christ’s physical death, in order to present them holy and blameless before him, provided they keep firmly to the gospel they heard. Paul rejoices in suffering for their sake, sharing in the hardships that come to Christ’s people, as the servant entrusted with making God’s word fully known. That word is a mystery hidden for ages and now revealed: Christ among the Gentiles, and in them, the hope of glory. Paul proclaims Christ, warning and teaching everyone, to present everyone mature in him, and he labours at it with the energy Christ supplies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery of Christ in You: Union with Christ as the Heart of the Gospel

The phrase “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (v. 27) is the most compressed statement of the doctrine of union with Christ in the New Testament. The mystery that was hidden for ages is not merely that Gentiles would be included in the covenant people (though that is part of it); it is that Christ himself would take up residence in his people — that the indwelling of the Spirit would mean the indwelling of Christ himself in the hearts of those who believe. Reformed theology has always understood union with Christ as the foundation of all soteriological benefits: it is because believers are in Christ that they are justified, sanctified, and will be glorified. And it is because Christ is in believers that they have the living presence of the hope of glory dwelling within them now.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that they needed additional spiritual experiences and esoteric knowledge to be “complete” or “mature.” Paul says: the mystery that makes for maturity is already in you. Christ in you is the hope of glory. The treasure the false teachers are selling is already yours, in a far more intimate and certain form than they can offer. Now: The believer who feels spiritually incomplete, who is seeking a second blessing, a higher experience, a deeper initiation, needs to hear this: Christ is in you. The one in whom all fullness dwells is dwelling in you by his Spirit. The seeking is not wrong; but what you are seeking is already present. Seek to know more fully the one who is already yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,

And you. Key words. From the cosmic to the personal. The great reconciliation includes you.

Who once were alienated. Key words. “Alienated” (apallotrioō, estranged, made strangers). Cut off from God (Ephesians 2:12; 4:18).

And hostile in mind. Key words. Enemies of God in their thinking (Romans 8:7). Not neutral, but opposed.

Doing evil deeds. Key words. Their hostility showed in their actions. This was the Colossians’ condition, and everyone’s, before Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers are as bad as they could be. It means they are alienated from God and opposed to him at heart.

In a sentence. Once you were alienated from God and were enemies in your minds because of your evil behaviour.

For worship. Remember what you were, and thank God for what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,

He has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death. Key words. In his real, physical body, which died. The false teachers may have despised the body; Paul stresses that reconciliation happened through Christ’s flesh and blood.

In order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him. Key words. The goal: on the last day, believers will stand before God holy (set apart), blameless (without blemish, like an unblemished sacrifice), and above reproach (with no accusation that can stand). Through Christ’s work, not their own (Ephesians 5:27; Jude 24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are now sinless. It means God will present them so, perfected in Christ.

In a sentence. But now he has reconciled you by Christ’s physical body through death to present you holy in his sight, without blemish and free from accusation,

For worship. One day you will stand before God holy and blameless, because of Christ. Praise him.

verseByVerse.quote: if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.

If indeed you continue in the faith. Key words. A condition. “Continue” (epimenō, remain, persist). The faith: both their believing and the gospel believed.

Stable and steadfast. Key words. “Stable” (tethemeliōmenoi, founded, like a building on its foundation). “Steadfast” (hedraioi, firm, settled).

Not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard. Key words. “Shifting” (metakineō, being moved away). The danger: being drawn away by false teaching.

Which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven. Key words. The gospel has gone throughout the world: it is not a secret teaching.

And of which I, Paul, became a minister. Key words. Paul’s calling.

Where Christians differ: does this condition mean believers can lose salvation? Some read “if you continue” as showing that true believers may fall away and be lost. Verdict: Perseverance is the evidence of genuine faith, and the warning is one of God’s means of producing it. Those who are truly reconciled will continue, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). Those who finally abandon the faith show they never truly had it (1 John 2:19). The condition is real and must be heard; it is how God keeps his people steadfast (Westminster 17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our own strength. It means true faith endures, by God’s grace.

In a sentence. if you continue in your faith, established and firm, and do not move from the hope held out in the gospel. This is the gospel that you heard and that has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and of which Paul has become a servant.

On a Tuesday. Stay grounded in the gospel you first believed. Do not drift after novelties.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,

Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake. Key words. Paul is in prison; he rejoices because his suffering serves the church.

And in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions. Key words. “Afflictions” (thlipseis): the word is never used of Christ’s atoning death. Paul does not mean Christ’s atoning suffering was incomplete; he means the sufferings that Christ’s people must endure as they carry the gospel to the world. Christ suffers in his people (Acts 9:4). There is an appointed measure of suffering for the church before the end, and Paul gladly takes his share.

For the sake of his body, that is, the church. Key words. His suffering builds up the church.

Where Christians differ: the merits of the saints. Roman Catholic teaching has used this verse to support a treasury of merit: the sufferings of saints added to Christ’s, applied to others through indulgences. Verdict: Christ’s atoning work was complete and finished (John 19:30; Hebrews 10:14). Nothing can be added to it. Paul’s sufferings did not atone for anyone; they were the cost of bringing the gospel to them. There is no treasury of merit and no need for indulgences.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering earns salvation. It means suffering for Christ serves the church.

In a sentence. Now Paul rejoices in what he is suffering for you, and he fills up in his flesh what is still lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions, for the sake of his body, which is the church.

For worship. If you suffer for Christ and his church, rejoice. Your suffering is not wasted.
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not mean Christ’s atoning suffering was incomplete; he shares in the afflictions that Christ’s people must still endure.

verseByVerse.quote: of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.

Of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you. Key words. “Stewardship” (oikonomia, management of a household, a trust). God entrusted Paul with the gospel for the Gentiles.

To make the word of God fully known. Key words. “Fully known” (plēroō, fulfil, complete). To proclaim it completely and spread it everywhere.

The mystery hidden for ages and generations. Key words. A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God (Ephesians 3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26). Not a secret for an elite, as in the mystery religions and the false teaching, but God’s plan now made public.

But now revealed to his saints. Key words. To all believers, not just an inner circle.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament was silent about it. The prophets hinted at it, but it was not fully understood until Christ.

In a sentence. Paul has become its servant by the commission God gave him to present to you the word of God in its fullness: the mystery that has been kept hidden for ages and generations, but is now disclosed to the Lord’s people.

On a Tuesday. God’s great mystery has been revealed to you. Share it with someone who does not know.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.

To them God chose to make known. Key words. God’s free choice to reveal it.

How great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery. Key words. The astonishing part: the Gentiles are included.

Which is Christ in you. Key words. The mystery revealed: Christ himself dwelling in Gentile believers by his Spirit. “In you” is plural: among you, and in each of you. The Messiah of Israel living in pagans who had been without hope.

The hope of glory. Key words. Christ in you now guarantees glory to come: resurrection, glorification, sharing his glory (3:4; Romans 8:17–18). The present indwelling is the pledge of future glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers become divine. It means Christ dwells in them by the Spirit, uniting them to himself.

In a sentence. To them God has chosen to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.

For worship. Christ is in you, the hope of glory. Rejoice in that today.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.

Him we proclaim. Key words. Not a system, not rules, not experiences, but a person: Christ.

Warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom. Key words. “Warning” (noutheteō, admonish, counsel, correct). “Teaching” (didaskō). Both negative and positive. With all wisdom: skilfully, fitting the truth to people. “Everyone” three times: unlike the false teachers, who offered maturity only to an elite, Paul offers it to all.

That we may present everyone mature in Christ. Key words. “Mature” (teleios, complete, perfect, the word the mystery religions used for initiates). True maturity is not initiation into secrets, but growth in Christ. The goal of ministry: to present every believer mature to God on the last day.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers reach sinless perfection. It means growth to maturity in Christ.

In a sentence. He is the one we proclaim, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone fully mature in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Whom are you helping to grow toward maturity in Christ? Warn and teach with wisdom and love.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.

For this I toil. Key words. “Toil” (kopiaō, labour to exhaustion).

Struggling. Key words. “Struggling” (agōnizomai, contending, as an athlete in the games, from which agony).

With all his energy that he powerfully works within me. Key words. “Energy” (energeia) and “works” (energeō). Paul works hard, and every bit of it is Christ’s power working in him. The same balance as Philippians 2:12–13. Ministry is strenuous, but the strength is Christ’s.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did nothing. He toiled. It means his toil was powered by Christ.

In a sentence. To this end Paul strenuously contends with all the energy Christ so powerfully works in him.

For worship. Ask Christ to work powerfully in you, and then work hard by his strength.
